title: Children
hookLine: children are gifts, and teachers too
tomorrow: what do you owe a parent when it's complicated?

cards: Get down to a four-year-old's height and the room changes. Table edges at eye level. The underside of everything.

Grown-ups turn into knees and voices from somewhere above. So why would Jesus tell grown-ups to become like children? In Matthew, his friends ask him a status question: who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?
He doesn't answer with a name. He calls a little child over and stands the child in the middle of them.

teach.b: Then he says it, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "unless you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven."
And he explains what he means: whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest. Not cute. Not naive.
Small, and fine with it. A child can't earn the room's respect or win the argument, and still asks for what she needs. Notice how physical Jesus is about this.
In Mark, people bring children to him, and the disciples try to send them away. Jesus is displeased. Let them come, he says.
Then, in the Douay-Rheims words: "embracing them, and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them."
Arms, hands, a blessing you can feel. The Church keeps that touch. At a Catholic baptism, the priest traces a small cross on the child's forehead, and then the parents and godparents do the same.
Some Catholic parents still trace that cross on their kids' foreheads at bedtime.
And the Catechism has a line worth repeating tonight: a child is not something owed to anyone, but a gift. So children are gifts, and here they're teachers too. Jesus didn't explain greatness.
He pointed at a child and let the child be the lesson.

games.q: at a family dinner, your seven-year-old cousin keeps asking "but why?" about grace before the meal while the adults shush her. going by Mark 10, what fits?
o: shush her kindly; kids should watch and learn first.
let her ask, and answer her at her own height.
tell her it's a grown-up thing she'll get later.
games.why: in Mark, the disciples try to send the children away and Jesus is displeased: let them come. the questions are part of coming.

practice: Lower yourself for this sit: sit on the floor, or kneel, or crouch with a hand on a chair. Look around the room from down there, at the things that tower and the things you never see from standing.

Stay low, breathe, and let a child's-eye view be the teacher for a while. If there's a child in your life, bring back the last question they asked you that you rushed past, and give it your whole attention now.

wordCard.voice: Children. Gifts, not something owed, and in Matthew, the lesson itself, standing in the middle of the room. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew's word for the little child Jesus stands in the middle.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: a child teaches, if the grown-ups get low enough to learn. That's day one thousand six hundred fifty-six.
